overview: Accordant Group is a New Zealand-listed staffing and recruitment holding company (formerly AWF Madison Group, renamed October 2020) operating a multi-brand portfolio: AWF (blue-collar/industrial labour hire), Madison Recruitment and Absolute IT (white-collar temp/contract/permanent recruitment, including IT), and JacksonStone & Partners and Hobson Leavy (executive search). The Group is 100% New Zealand-domiciled, generating revenue almost entirely from temporary/contract labour placement fees with smaller permanent-placement and retained executive-search fees, and is highly geared to the NZ labour market cycle. FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026) revenue was $165.1m (flat vs FY2025's $165.2m) with a net loss after tax of $2.1m, an improvement on FY2025's $2.9m loss but still the third straight loss-making year after a severe two-year downturn (revenue fell from $227.4m in FY2023 to $165.2m in FY2025).

businessModel.summary: Accordant earns margin (a spread between what it bills clients and what it pays workers/contractors) on temporary and contract labour placements, plus one-off placement fees for permanent recruitment and retained fees for executive search. The vast majority of revenue is temporary/contract-based (~80%), meaning revenue is largely transactional and reprices immediately with hours worked and headcount on assignment, not a recurring/subscription model. Two reporting segments: Blue Collar (AWF industrial/trades labour hire) and White Collar (Madison, Absolute IT, JacksonStone & Partners, Hobson Leavy - temp, contract, permanent and executive search).

revenue_streams.name: White Collar (Madison/Absolute IT/JacksonStone/Hobson Leavy) - temp, contract, permanent, executive search

businessModel.customer_type: B2B - public sector (government/local government, historically a significant share) and private sector across infrastructure, construction, logistics, manufacturing, professional services and technology; no single customer exceeds 10% of Group revenue (low customer concentration risk)
businessModel.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand (one geographical segment); national footprint of ~20 AWF branches plus white-collar offices in Auckland, Wellington, Hamilton, Christchurch and other centres

main_competitors: Korn Ferry / global executive search firms (for Hobson Leavy/JacksonStone)
in-house/direct-sourcing by large corporates and government (structural competitor to all recruiters)
competitivePosition.market_position: AWF describes itself as New Zealand's largest blue-collar labour hire provider by scale/branch network; Madison and Absolute IT are mid-tier generalist/IT recruiters; JacksonStone & Partners and Hobson Leavy are boutique executive search firms. The multi-brand model gives Accordant broader sector and role-level diversification than most single-brand NZ competitors, but no brand holds a dominant, defensible share nationally, and several competitors are larger global players (Randstad, Hays, Korn Ferry) with greater scale and balance sheet strength.

moat_factors.description: AWF (est. 1988) and Madison (est. 1998) have long operating histories, health & safety accreditations (ACC Accredited Employer, Tōtika Gold), and industry awards that support client trust in a relationship-driven industry

AWF's ~20-branch footprint from Kaitaia to Invercargill is a genuine cost and service advantage in blue-collar labour hire versus smaller regional operators, supporting tender wins for large infrastructure/logistics clients

Spanning blue-collar labour hire through to C-suite executive search cushions the Group when any single segment or client type (e.g. government) is weak, as evidenced by Hobson Leavy's resilience offsetting Absolute IT/Madison weakness in FY24-25
Recruitment is a low-switching-cost, commoditised service for most clients; preferred supplier panels can be lost or won relatively easily, and clients can multi-source across agencies

Labour hire licensing requirements are low in NZ; new entrants and offshore players can compete relatively freely, though the new government procurement 'economic benefit to NZ test' offers Accordant a modest edge over foreign-owned competitors for public tenders

weaknesses: No durable structural moat - the business is essentially a people-and-relationships model with thin operating margins and high operating leverage to volumes
Heavy historical reliance on government/public-sector spending (JacksonStone, Madison, Absolute IT all cited government spending cuts as a major FY24-25 headwind)
Small scale relative to global competitors (Randstad, Hays, Korn Ferry) limits investment capacity in technology/AI and pricing power
Balance sheet weakened by the downturn (elevated leverage), constraining ability to invest in growth or withstand a further shock
Market capitalisation of only ~NZ$10-15m and very thin trading liquidity limit access to capital and institutional investor interest

growthDrivers: Cyclical recovery in NZ labour market - unemployment appears to be peaking/plateauing and job-advertising volumes, tender activity and business confidence were improving through FY26, particularly in H2
Blue-collar (AWF) momentum in civil infrastructure and logistics sectors, with management citing 'stronger momentum' entering FY27 and a strengthened sales/tender pipeline

White-collar segment returned to a positive profit contribution in FY26 after a FY25 loss, with retained/executive-search revenue (Hobson Leavy, JacksonStone) up 52.8%, the most resilient and highest-margin part of the portfolio
AI/automation investment (180+ CRM automations, candidate-facing AI agents, AI assistants across all business units) aimed at productivity and margin improvement rather than headcount growth
New government procurement 'economic benefit to New Zealand' test structurally favours locally-domiciled Accordant over foreign-owned competitors for public-sector tenders
New foothold in health-sector talent solutions (Madison) and diversification into higher-margin senior/specialist and contingent workforce segments

Balance sheet repair via the May 2026 $5m+ capital raise and extended, more favourable bank facility (to April 2028) removes near-term financial distress overhang and could re-rate the stock if earnings recover
Long-run structural NZ skills shortages and an ageing workforce support secular demand for staffing/contingent labour intermediaries

keyRisks.detail: Revenue and profit are highly correlated with GDP, business confidence and unemployment; the FY23-FY25 downturn saw Group revenue fall ~27% (from $227.4m to $165.2m) and NPAT swing from a $2.0m profit to losses of up to $10.0m (FY24, impairment-driven), illustrating severe operating leverage in both directions

keyRisks.risk: NZ macro conditions and immigration/government policy
keyRisks.detail: As a 100%-NZ business with no geographic diversification, Accordant is entirely exposed to the domestic economic cycle, interest rates, and government fiscal policy; sharp cuts to government spending post-2023 election materially hit JacksonStone, Absolute IT and Madison's public-sector revenue, and immigration settings affect both labour supply for AWF and net demand for local recruitment

keyRisks.risk: Client concentration by sector, not single-customer
keyRisks.detail: No single customer exceeds 10% of revenue (low single-name concentration), but there is meaningful concentration by sector (construction, government, IT) and by client type (public sector), so policy or sector-specific downturns can hit multiple business units simultaneously, as seen in FY24-25

keyRisks.risk: Balance sheet and bank covenant stress
keyRisks.detail: Net bank debt of $28.5m against equity of only $17.9m at FY26 year-end (debt/equity ratio reported at 2.85x as of Sept 2025) forced a rights issue in April-May 2026 to raise a minimum $5.0m (up to $6.7m target) at $0.15/share, a deeply dilutive raise (1.269 new shares per existing share) which diluted non-participating shareholders; the raise was needed to secure covenant relief and extend banking facilities to April 2028 - the company was under real financial pressure, not routine refinancing

No interim or final dividend has been paid since FY2023 (dividend suspended amid the downturn); FY2025 and FY2026 both saw nil interim and nil final dividends, removing the income-return component of the investment case indefinitely until profitability and debt reduction are achieved

Segment profit margins are low single digits (Blue Collar segment profit of $2.1m on $77.3m revenue = ~2.7%; White Collar $1.1m on $87.9m = ~1.2% in FY26), meaning small revenue swings cause outsized swings in profitability, and central costs/finance costs ($3.0m FY26) must be covered before any net profit

Recruitment/staffing is a fragmented, low-barrier-to-entry industry with larger global players (Randstad, Hays, Korn Ferry), niche local boutiques, and increasing direct-sourcing/in-house talent acquisition by large employers all competing for the same client relationships, limiting long-term pricing power

Goodwill of $31.6m and other indefinite-life intangibles of $12.1m remain on the balance sheet (Madison and JacksonStone CGUs flagged as a Key Audit Matter in FY26); a failure to achieve forecast recovery could trigger further impairments as occurred in FY24 ($11.0m impairment across Madison and AWF)

keyRisks.risk: AI/technology disruption to entry-level and administrative roles
keyRisks.detail: Management has explicitly flagged that AI tools are already reducing demand for entry-level IT and administrative/clerical roles (a core Madison and Absolute IT market), which could structurally shrink parts of the addressable market even as the cycle recovers

The Hull family (founder) is the largest shareholder and provided top-up support for the FY2026 capital raise; a portion of shareholders chose not to participate and were diluted, creating potential governance/register tension and signalling constrained broader investor appetite for the stock

recentDevelopments.event: FY2026 results: revenue $165.1m (flat YoY), net loss after tax $2.1m (improved from $2.9m loss in FY25); net operating cashflow improved to $1.6m (from -$0.6m); net bank debt $28.5m; no interim or final dividend declared

Capital raise completed - minimum $5.0m target achieved via renounceable rights offer at $0.15/share (1.269 new shares per existing share, up to $6.7m targeted); Hull Family Trust committed $3.25m; proceeds used to reduce bank debt and secure improved banking terms/covenants

Renounceable rights offer conducted on NZX (rights quoted 17-30 April 2026); bank agreed to extend facility terms to April 2028 with covenants based on cumulative EBITDA, leverage ratio and interest cover, conditional on the raise succeeding
Board streamlined following the capital raise, with departures of non-executive directors reported post-completion

Revenue declined 8% YoY to $82.0m (a marked improvement on the 21% decline in H1 FY25); net loss after tax narrowed to $1.1m from $1.4m; white-collar segment returned to a $0.4m profit from a $0.3m loss; no interim dividend declared; debt/equity ratio reported at 2.85x, up from 2.67x at March 2025
Annual Shareholder Meeting - CEO reiterated commitment to enduring economic conditions and financial discipline; AI assistants rolled out across all business units

FY2025 results: revenue $165.2m (-22% YoY... actually -22% vs FY24's $212.4m); net loss after tax $2.9m (improved from $10.0m loss in FY24); no dividend; management flagged FY27 as the expected year for a return to prior trading levels

FY2024 net loss of $10.0m driven substantially by non-cash goodwill impairments of $6.5m (Madison) and $4.5m (AWF) due to a deteriorating demand outlook, on top of a 6.6% revenue decline to $212.4m; dividend suspended

bullCase: Balance sheet risk has been materially reduced by the May 2026 capital raise and the extension of bank facilities to April 2028 on improved covenant terms, removing the most acute near-term financial distress overhang

Signs of cyclical bottoming - H2 FY26 showed improving momentum across AWF (civil/infrastructure, logistics), Madison (temp recruitment) and JacksonStone (contracting activity), with management citing a 'good start to FY27'

White-collar segment returned to profitability in FY26 after a FY25 loss, and the highest-margin retained/executive-search revenue (Hobson Leavy, JacksonStone) grew strongly (+52.8%), improving overall business mix

Deeply depressed valuation (market cap ~NZ$10-15m, trading well below historical shareholders' funds levels of $30m+) offers optionality if NZ labour market conditions normalise and the Group returns to its historical mid-cycle earnings capability

Diversified multi-brand model across blue-collar, white-collar and executive search provides some natural hedge across the economic cycle and positions the Group to capture share as smaller/less resilient competitors consolidate or exit
bearCase: The FY26 capital raise was dilutive (1.269 new shares per existing share at $0.15) and driven by necessity (elevated debt/equity of 2.85x) rather than growth funding, and a portion of shareholders were unable or unwilling to participate, diluting them further and creating an overhang of investor distrust

Three consecutive years of net losses (FY24: -$10.0m including impairment; FY25: -$2.9m; FY26: -$2.1m) with no dividend since FY2023 mean the investment thesis relies entirely on an uncertain and already twice-delayed cyclical recovery (management flagged FY27 as the 'return to normal' year back in FY25, and is now again pointing to FY27/FY28)

Thin, single-digit segment margins and high fixed/finance costs mean any renewed NZ economic softness, a delayed rate-cutting cycle, or a stall in government spending recovery could quickly push the Group back into deeper losses and revisit covenant stress

$31.6m of goodwill and $12.1m of other intangibles remain on a $17.9m equity base; Madison and JacksonStone were flagged as a Key Audit Matter, meaning any shortfall versus recovery forecasts could trigger further material impairments

Structurally challenged segments (entry-level IT and administrative/clerical roles at Absolute IT and Madison) face secular AI-driven demand erosion even as the cyclical downturn eases, and the business has no exposure outside New Zealand to diversify this risk
moatRating: none - Accordant operates in a fragmented, low-switching-cost, labour-intensive staffing market with no meaningful network effects, brand lock-in, or regulatory protection; its multi-brand diversification and NZ branch network provide modest scale/service advantages but do not constitute a durable competitive moat, evidenced by persistent thin margins and severe earnings cyclicality
cyclicalityNote: Highly cyclical. Group NPAT swung from a peak of $6.2m in FY2021 (COVID-era demand surge) down to a trough net loss of $10.0m in FY2024 (which included $11.0m of non-cash goodwill impairment; underlying trading loss was smaller) - a peak-to-trough swing of roughly $16m on a business with historical shareholders' funds of only $20-37m. Revenue fell from a post-COVID peak of $227.4m in FY2023 to $165.1-165.2m in FY2025/FY26, a ~27% decline. Pre-impairment 'normal' cycle NPAT has ranged from roughly $2.0m (FY2019, FY2023 troughs) up to $6.2m (FY2021 peak), while FY2025-FY26 losses of $2.1-2.9m represent a deeper-than-typical cyclical trough, reflecting the severity and duration of the 2023-2026 NZ labour market downturn compared to prior cycles.
